content: 1. Active case finding (ACF) for tuberculosis (TB) has demonstrated advantages over passive case finding, particularly when conducted at the household level rather than in health facility settings. This approach reduces barriers such as long waiting times at clinics and the financial burden associated with seeking treatment. 2. ACF has been shown to increase knowledge about TB, although the confidence in this evidence is very low. 3. ACF does not appear to increase stigma associated with TB. However, enhanced case finding strategies, such as screening of migrants, have received mixed reviews regarding their impact on stigma. The confidence in this evidence is very low. 4. Enhanced case finding can lead to increased anxiety among individuals due to fears of the consequences of a positive test result, such as stigma, deportation (for migrants), or punishment. Anxiety may also stem from the perception of the health system as authoritative. The confidence in this evidence is low. 5. Women participating in enhanced case finding strategies that require multiple visits to health facilities have reported conflicts in their relationships. Husbands were described as aggressive, angry, or suspicious of infidelity, perceiving the freedom to visit facilities on consecutive days as an opportunity to meet other men. The confidence in this evidence is very low. 6. Feelings of dependence and vulnerability have been reported by individuals undergoing ACF or enhanced case finding strategies, particularly when they require financial assistance or help navigating systems such as overcoming language barriers. The confidence in this evidence is low. 7. Positive mental health outcomes have been associated with ACF and enhanced case finding (ECF), including feelings of being cared for by those conducting the activities and increased understanding and acceptance of people living with TB. The confidence in this evidence is low. 8. Systematic screening for TB among household and close contacts of TB patients is strongly recommended, with moderate certainty of evidence. This recommendation is based on the high risk of TB infection and disease development in these groups, as well as the reduction in mortality and increase in case detection associated with systematic screening. 9. Screening for TB among household contacts can be conducted at the patient’s home or in a clinic setting. However, household-based screening is preferred to ensure a higher proportion of contacts are reached and to reduce barriers to accessing care. 10. The most accurate screening and diagnostic algorithms should be used for high-risk groups, such as household contacts of TB patients, to maximize the effectiveness of the intervention. 11. Monitoring and evaluation of TB screening interventions are essential for assessing their performance. Standard procedures can be complemented by operational research to improve local implementation and contribute to the global evidence base. 12. Further research is needed to optimize the implementation of contact screening, including strategies to maximize reach, ensure follow-up for diagnostic evaluation, and initiate preventive treatment for contacts without active TB disease. 13. Screening approaches vary in feasibility. Symptom-based screening is highly feasible in most settings, while chest radiography (CXR) screening is less feasible, particularly in household settings. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs) can be feasible with remote sputum collection and sample transport, provided resources are available. 14. People in prisons are at significantly higher risk for TB, with an estimated incidence 23 times higher than the general population. Systematic screening for active TB in prisons is recommended, although the quality of evidence is very low. 15. Observational data from prison settings indicate that symptom-based screening, CXR, and mWRDs have varying levels of effectiveness and feasibility depending on the TB burden in the setting. For example, mWRDs have shown high effectiveness in moderate and medium burden settings. 16. The WHO emphasizes the importance of using the most accurate screening and diagnostic algorithms possible in high-risk groups, such as prisoners and household contacts, to ensure effective TB detection and management.
